body:
### Pandas version checks

- [X] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [X] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import csv

import pandas as pd

from io import StringIO
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

d = {'col1': [1, 2], 'col2': [3, 4]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data=d)

# define custom insert method for to_sql as written in documentation https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/io.html?highlight=synchronize#insertion-method

def psql_insert_copy(table, conn, keys, data_iter):
    """
    Execute SQL statement inserting data

    Parameters
    ----------
    table : pandas.io.sql.SQLTable
    conn : sqlalchemy.engine.Engine or sqlalchemy.engine.Connection
    keys : list of str
        Column names
    data_iter : Iterable that iterates the values to be inserted
    """
    # gets a DBAPI connection that can provide a cursor
    dbapi_conn = conn.connection
    with dbapi_conn.cursor() as cur:
        s_buf = StringIO()
        writer = csv.writer(s_buf)
        writer.writerows(data_iter)
        s_buf.seek(0)

        columns = ', '.join(['"{}"'.format(k) for k in keys])
        if table.schema:
            table_name = '{}.{}'.format(table.schema, table.name)
        else:
            table_name = table.name

        sql = 'COPY {} ({}) FROM STDIN WITH CSV'.format(
            table_name, columns)
        cur.copy_expert(sql=sql, file=s_buf)

# you need to have PostgreSQL running and give correct credentials here to reproduce the issue
engine = create_engine(f'postgresql://{'user'}:{'password'}@{'host'}/{'db'}')

with engine.connect() as conn:
     df.to_sql('target_table', 
               con=conn,
               schema='public',
               if_exists='append',
               index=False,
               method=psql_insert_copy)
```


### Issue Description

When I use custom method for PostgreSQL in `DataFrame.to_sql`according to the [docummentation ](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/user_guide/io.html?highlight=synchronize#insertion-method), the table is created with correct column names and numeric types (if it doesn't exist) but no values are imported (table is empty), no warning or error is raised in pandas nor in the database.

It works in `pandas~=1.3.5` and breaks when `1.4.0` or `1.4.1` is installed (keeping sqlalchemy and psycopg2 on same versions). I am suspecting something related to the change that `to_sql` can now return an Int value instead or None, but couldn't find how that is related or how it can be fixed.

### Expected Behavior

Full `df` is imported into the table including its values.

title: BUG: Inconsistent resampling behaviour
body:
- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.

- [ ] (optional) I have confirmed this bug exists on the master branch of pandas.

---

Attached below is my code for extracting processing financial tick data from the MetaTrader5 application:

```python
def CollectTicks(Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute, CurrencyPair, Digits, ResampleOffset = None):

    StartTime = datetime.datetime(Year, Month, Day, Hour, Minute).timestamp() #Convert the start time to epoch time

    EndTime = StartTime + 604800 #Add 1 week to the start time and set the result as the end time

    Ticks = mt5.copy_ticks_range(CurrencyPair, StartTime, EndTime, mt5.COPY_TICKS_ALL) #Retrieve the ticks from the start time until the end time

    BreakFlag = False #Set the break flag to false

    while(True):

        StartTime = EndTime #Set the prevous end time as the new start time

        EndTime = StartTime + 604800 #Add 1 week to the new start time and set the result as the new end time

        if(EndTime > time.time()): #If the end time is more than the current time

            EndTime = time.time() #Set the end time as the current time

            BreakFlag = True #Set the break flag to true

        NewTicks = mt5.copy_ticks_range(CurrencyPair, StartTime, EndTime, mt5.COPY_TICKS_ALL) #Retrive the new ticks with the new start time and new end time

        Ticks = np.hstack((Ticks, NewTicks)) #Cocatenate the newly retrieved ticks with the previously retrieved ticks

        if(BreakFlag == True): #If the break flag is set to true

            break #Exit the loop

    TickDataframe = pd.DataFrame(Ticks) #Covert the ticks array to a dataframe

    TickDataframe.drop(["time", "last", "volume", "flags", "volume_real"], axis = 1, inplace = True) #Drop the unwanted columns from the dataframe

    TickDataframe["time_msc"] = pd.to_datetime(TickDataframe["time_msc"], unit = "ms") #Convert the milisecond timestap to the epoch date time

    TickDataframe.set_index("time_msc", inplace = True) #Set the milisecond time column as the dataframe's index

    TickDataframe.round(Digits) #Round all values in the dataframe to the desired number of digits

    TickDataframe["mid"] = round(((TickDataframe["bid"] + TickDataframe["ask"]) / 2.0), Digits) #Generate the mid dataframe and round it to (Digits) figures

    if(ResampleOffset != None): #If the ResampleOffset input is not None

        CandleCloses = {} #Instantiate a dictionary

        CandleCloses["Bid Closes"] = TickDataframe["bid"].resample(ResampleOffset).ohlc().close.dropna().to_numpy() #Resample the bid ticks to create bid candles based on the resample offset and convert it into a numpy array

        CandleCloses["Ask Closes"] = TickDataframe["ask"].resample(ResampleOffset).ohlc().close.dropna().to_numpy() #Resample the ask ticks to create ask candles based on the resample offset and convert it into a numpy array

        CandleCloses["Mid Closes"] = TickDataframe["mid"].resample(ResampleOffset).ohlc().close.dropna().to_numpy() #Resample the mid ticks to create mid candles based on the resample offset and convert it into a numpy array

        return CandleCloses #Return the dictionary containing candle closes

    else: #If the ResampleOffset input is None

        return TickDataframe #Return the dataframe of ticks

```

#### Problem description

After resampling the collected tick data with the "1Min" offset, the resampled data for 2 different instruments have a different number of candles even when their time indexes cover the same date range.

title: Resource DX: type-safe access to `Resource#value`
body:
### Which @angular/* package(s) are relevant/related to the feature request? core ### Description The idea is to prevent accessing `Resource#value` while the resource is in `'error'` status at the type level. Runtime errors would become almost impossible. ## Current behavior Today, `resource.value()` **throws** when status is `'error'`, but TypeScript still allows **unguarded** reads, for example: ```ts // Compiles today; may throw at runtime when status is 'error' console.log(userRes.value().name); ``` Common **safe** patterns require an explicit guard first: 1. **Guard inside a `computed` (or other reactive context)** ```ts const name = computed(() => userRes.hasValue() ? userRes.value().name : ''); ``` 2. **Treat status + value as one compound state** - guard in TypeScript and in templates: ```ts function printName(userRes: Resource<{name: string}>) { if (userRes.hasValue()) { console.log(userRes.value().name); } } ``` ```html @if (userRes.hasValue()) {

{{ userRes.value().name }}

} ``` The problem is that **today’s types do not enforce those guards**: developers must be disciplined and repeat them everywhere. Unguarded reads compile and only fail at runtime — often far from where the read was written. ### Proposed solution Model `Resource` at the type level as a **discriminated shape aligned with `ResourceSnapshot`**: With `status` being set to `error`, the `value` property does not exist. That **forces type narrowing** before using `value()` — for example with `hasValue()`. Unguarded `userRes.value()` would be a type error; the guarded patterns above stay valid. Caveats: Someone can still capture `userRes.value()` into a local in a narrowed branch and misuse it later—that class of mistake exists for many APIs and cannot be fully ruled out by types. --- Scope of typing changes: Only the **status-sensitive surface** needs to change (how `value`, `status`, and `error` relate); other members of `Resource` can stay as they are. This is likely a **breaking change for typings**; it is easier to justify while `resource` is still **experimental**. ### Alternatives considered Stay as it is and stick to the mentioned common safe patterns.

title: JIT application ignores NgModule providers from AOT-compiled library imported through a standalone component
body:
### Which @angular/* package(s) are the source of the bug?

Don't known / other

### Is this a regression?

No

### Description

When a JIT-compiled Angular application consumes a library compiled in AOT mode, providers defined in an NgModule may not be registered.

In the affected scenario, both the standalone component and the service are defined in the AOT-compiled library. The standalone component imports an NgModule from the same library, and that module provides a service.

When the standalone component is used from a JIT application, Angular fails to resolve the service dependency because the provider is not registered in any injector.

### Expected behavior

Providers defined in an NgModule imported by a standalone component should be registered regardless of the compilation mode of the consuming application.

The behavior should be consistent across:
- JIT application + JIT library
- AOT application + AOT library
- JIT application + AOT library

### Actual behavior

In the JIT application + AOT library scenario:

- Angular successfully processes the standalone component and its imports;
- providers defined in imported NgModules are not registered;
- dependency injection fails when Angular attempts to instantiate the standalone component.

### Additional observations

The issue appears specific to the JIT consumer + AOT library combination.

The same reproduction works if:
- the consuming application is compiled in AOT mode;
- the service is provided directly by the standalone component instead of by the imported NgModule.

This suggests that provider metadata originating from NgModule is not correctly propagated when processed by the JIT runtime from an AOT-compiled library.

title: Signal Forms / FormValueControl violates ControlValueAccessor contract by calling writeValue back after onChange, causing infinite loop
body:
### Which @angular/* package(s) are the source of the bug?

forms

### Is this a regression?

No

### Description

Signal forms break the one-way `ControlValueAccessor` contract by calling `writeValue` back on a CVA component after that component called `onChange`, directly contradicting Angular's own documentation.

### The documented contract

Angular's official documentation at angular.dev states clearly:

> **`writeValue(value: any): void`**
> Writes a new value to the element.
> This method is called by the forms API to write to the view when **programmatic changes from model to view** are requested.

This defines a strict one-way contract:

- `writeValue(value)` — called by the **form** for programmatic, external, model-to-view changes only
- `onChange(value)` — called by the **component** when the user changes the value (view-to-model)

These two directions must never form a loop. Angular's classic `FormControl` correctly respects this — calling `onChange` updates the `FormControl`'s internal value but does **not** trigger `writeValue` back on the CVA. Signal forms do not respect this.

### What Signal forms does wrong

When a CVA component bound via `[formField]` calls `onChange(value)`, the Signal form updates its internal signal. Because Signal form has no concept of **value origin** — it does not distinguish between a programmatic external `set()` and a value that just arrived from the CVA via `onChange` — it reactively pushes the value back to `writeValue` on the same CVA that just sent it:

```
User types in CVA component
  → onChange("hello") called
    → Signal form signal updates
      → writeValue("hello") called back on CVA  ← violates documented contract
```

The same issue applies to `FormValueControl`, the Signal form equivalent of CVA. There is no mechanism to indicate **who** submitted the change — whether it originated from inside the component or from an external model update. Without that distinction, any reactive form implementation will produce this loopback.

### Real-world impact

We implemented a CodeMirror editor as a `ControlValueAccessor`. CodeMirror manages its own internal document state. Our contract is:

- `writeValue` = programmatic value from outside, push into CodeMirror
- `onChange` = user edited the document, notify the form

When Signal form calls `writeValue` back after our `onChange`, we are forced to either:

1. **Compare the incoming `writeValue` value against CodeMirror's current document** to detect the loopback — an O(n) string comparison on every keystroke. For large documents exceeding 1MB this causes severe and measurable performance degradation.
2. **Use a dirty flag** to suppress the loopback `writeValue` — a workaround that should not be necessary and compensates for a broken contract.

Neither workaround is acceptable. `FormControl` does not require either. The behaviour difference between `FormControl` and Signal form for the same CVA implementation is a clear regression in the Signal form design.

### Expected behaviour

Signal form must not call `writeValue` on a CVA in response to a value that was just received from that same CVA's `onChange`. This is the documented contract and the behaviour `FormControl` has always correctly implemented.

title: apiserver: return 4xx instead of 500 for invalid kind type in version/kind decoding
body:
### What happened?

The Kubernetes API Server returns HTTP 500 Internal Server Error when handling a DELETE request whose request body contains an invalid `kind` field type.

In the following request, the `kind` field is set to a boolean value instead of a string. This is an invalid client request, but the API Server returns HTTP 500:

```bash
curl -X DELETE 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/apis/apiregistration.k8s.io/v1/apiservices' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"kind":true}'
```
Actual response:
```bash
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "couldn't get version/kind; json parse error: json: cannot unmarshal bool into Go struct field .kind of type string",
  "code": 500
}
```
A similar behavior can also be triggered on validatingwebhookconfigurations:
```bash
curl -X DELETE 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/apis/admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1/validatingwebhookconfigurations' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"kind":true}'
```
The response also returns HTTP 500 with the same kind of version/kind decoding error.

### What did you expect to happen?

```markdown
The API Server should treat this as an invalid client request and return a 4xx response, such as HTTP 400 Bad Request or HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity, instead of HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.

The response should report that the `kind` field has an invalid type, rather than exposing it as an internal server error.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start a Kubernetes cluster with Kubernetes v1.33.1.
2. Start the local API proxy:

```bash
kubectl proxy --port=8001
```
3. Send the following request:
```bash
curl -X DELETE 'http://127.0.0.1:8001/apis/apiregistration.k8s.io/v1/apiservices' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"kind":true}'
````
4.Observe that the API Server returns HTTP 500:
```bash
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "couldn't get version/kind; json parse error: json: cannot unmarshal bool into Go struct field .kind of type string",
  "code": 500
}
```

### Anything else we need to know?

```markdown
This issue was found during RESTful API fuzzing of the Kubernetes API Server.

The request body is clearly malformed because `kind` should be a string. Therefore, the behavior appears to be an error classification problem: the invalid request is surfaced as an internal server error instead of a client-side validation or decoding error.

In my test, this behavior is reproducible on Kubernetes v1.33.1.

Kubernetes v1.33.1

title: DRA: Scheduler CEL evaluation fails with "no such key" when accessing nested attributes without existence check
body:
### What happened?

I am using DRA with a CEL selector to filter devices based on driver attributes. When writing an expression that accesses a nested field within `device.attributes`, the scheduler encounters a CEL runtime error if the specific driver key does not exist on the device, rather than evaluating the expression to false.

The following expression fails during the DynamicResources filter plugin execution:

```
cel:
  expression: 'device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].sharingStrategy == "runai-fractions"'
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the expression to evaluate to false for devices that do not possess the gpu.nvidia.com attribute, allowing the scheduler to simply skip those devices.

Instead, the scheduler treats this as a hard runtime error, preventing the claim from being allocated even if valid devices exist, or logging significant errors during the filter phase.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

```
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: DeviceClass
metadata:
  name: gpu.nvidia.com
spec:
  selectors:
  - cel: 
      expression: "device.driver == 'gpu.nvidia.com'"
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceSlice
metadata:
  name: kind-control-plane-gpu-devices-slice
spec:
  nodeName: kind-control-plane
  driver: gpu.nvidia.com

  pool:
    generation: 1
    resourceSliceCount: 1
    name: kind-control-plane-gpu-pool

  devices:
  - name: gpu-0
    bindsToNode: true

  - name: gpu-1
    attributes:
      sharingStrategy:
        string: runai-fractions
    bindsToNode: true
---
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1
kind: ResourceClaim
metadata:
  name: kind-control-plane-gpu-runai-fractionable-claim-1
spec:
  devices:
    requests:
    - name: gpu-runai-fractionable
      exactly:
        deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com
        capacity:
          requests:
            memory: 10Gi
        selectors:
        - cel:
            expression: 'device.attributes["gpu.nvidia.com"].sharingStrategy == "runai-fractions"'
---

  - name: fraction-container
    resources:
      claims:
      - name: fraction-claim
    image: ubuntu:latest
    command: [ "/bin/bash", "-c", "--" ]
    args: [sleep Infinity"]
```

title: DRA: partial prepare claims with different drivers can leave Pod stuck without rollback
body:
### What happened?

When a Pod depends on multiple ResourceClaims managed by different DRA drivers, prepare can succeed for one claim and fail for another.

In that case:
- one driver has already prepared its device and considers the claim successful
- another driver fails
- the Pod gets stuck in FailedPrepareDynamicResources
```
Warning  FailedPrepareDynamicResources  36s (x7 over 7m50s)  kubelet            Failed to prepare dynamic resources: prepare dynamic resources: NodePrepareResources failed for ResourceClaim fail-claim: intentional prepare failure for claim my-dra/fail-claim (995b7e92-9832-4cbf-9856-72be616486f4)
```
- no rollback happens for the driver that already succeeded

This can leave the Pod in a failed state while some devices remain prepared / reserved even though the Pod will never start.

### What did you expect to happen?

If any required claim fails during prepare, Kubernetes should eventually trigger cleanup for claims that were already successfully prepared for the same Pod.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run two different DRA drivers, each managing a different resource.
2. Create a Pod that requires both resources through separate claims.
3. Let prepare succeed for claim A and fail for claim B.
4. Observe that the Pod ends up in FailedPrepareDynamicResources, but claim A remains prepared.

### Anything else we need to know?

Depending on the driver implementation, this can effectively strand capacity and look like a device leak until some separate reconciliation cleans it up.

title: [Bug] kube-apiserver: `--audit-log-maxsize=0` does not disable rotation as documented, but defaults to 100MB via lumberjack**
body:
### What happened?

When configuring `kube-apiserver` with audit logging enabled, setting `--audit-log-maxsize=0` results in audit logs being rotated when they reach **100MB**, instead of growing indefinitely (or not rotating based on size) as implied by the documentation.

Since default values for `--audit-log-maxbackup` and `--audit-log-maxage` are also `0` (meaning "retain all" and "retain forever"), the result is not a single large file, but an accumulation of many 100MB log files until disk exhaustion.

### What did you expect to happen?

According to the `kube-apiserver` help text and documentation:

> `--audit-log-maxsize`: The maximum size in megabytes of the audit log file before it gets rotated. **If this is 0, the log file is not rotated.**

I expected the `audit.log` file to grow indefinitely without rotation when `maxsize` is set to `0`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start `kube-apiserver` with the following flags:
```bash
--audit-log-path=/tmp/k8s-audit.log
--audit-log-maxsize=0

```
2. Generate audit events sufficient to exceed 100MB (e.g., using a load testing tool or simply `dd` appending if testing the library directly, or heavy API usage).
3. Observe that the log file is rotated (renamed with a timestamp) once it hits approximately 100MB.

### Anything else we need to know?

The issue lies in the interaction between `k8s.io/apiserver` and the underlying logging library `gopkg.in/natefinch/lumberjack.v2`.

1. **Kubernetes Implementation**:
In `staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/plugin/pkg/audit/log/backend.go`, the backend is initialized with the user-provided `MaxSize`:
```go
func NewBackend(filename string, maxBackup, maxAge, maxSize int) audit.Backend {
    writer := &lumberjack.Logger{
        Filename:   filename,
        MaxSize:    maxSize,    // Passed as 0
        // ...
    }
    return backend.NewBackend(writer)
}

```


2. **Lumberjack Implementation**:
The `lumberjack` library treats `MaxSize: 0` not as "unlimited", but as "use default".
Reference: `lumberjack.go` in `natefinch/lumberjack`:
```go
const defaultMaxSize = 100 // megabytes

func (l *Logger) max() int64 {
    if l.MaxSize == 0 {
        return int64(defaultMaxSize * megabyte)
    }
    return int64(l.MaxSize) * int64(megabyte)
}

```
Consequently, passing `0` effectively sets the rotation threshold to 100MB.

title: kubectl apply --dry-run=client doesn't seem very dry
body:
### What happened? When I try to do some linting with `kubectl apply --dry-run=client` (with no config to simulate no available remote API) I first get ```console $ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -k overlays/preprod/ error: error validating "overlays/preprod/": error validating data: failed to download openapi: Get "http://localhost:8080/openapi/v2?timeout=32s": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused; if you choose to ignore these errors, turn validation off with --validate=false ``` This seems to make sense; and the [--validate](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/kubectl/generated/kubectl_apply/#options) docs seem reasonable in explaining `--validate=false` > "false" or "ignore" will not perform any schema validation, silently dropping any unknown or duplicate fields. Adding that flag, I a priori expected that I'd get some sort of "linting" that at least `kubectl` was parsing everything OK. However, it still fails ```console $ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -k overlays/preprod/ --validate=false -o yaml E0224 14:11:56.939647 112987 memcache.go:265] "Unhandled Error" err="couldn't get current server API group list: Get \"http://localhost:8080/api?timeout=32s\": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused" ... repeats, a lot ... unable to recognize "overlays/preprod/": Get "http://localhost:8080/api?timeout=32s": dial tcp 127.0.0.1:8080: connect: connection refused ... also repeats ... $ echo $? 1 ``` So with `--dry-run=client --validate=false` this is still trying to get to the API. Now I realise that AI is just regurgitating what it has seen and telling me what I want to hear, but perhaps that is illustrative that the broad consensus of what people _think_ this tool does. Note the documentation on `--dry-run` doesn't actually say this about API access > Must be "none", "server", or "client". If client strategy, only print the object that would be sent, without sending it. If server strategy, submit server-side request without persisting the resource. but it kind of _implies_ that it doesn't need API access. I'll be happy to propose a change with clarification of this, but I'd like to establish what the truth is before doing that :) Is it expected that `--dry-run=client` will not _send_ any information to the server, but still requires authenticated server access to complete successfully? What is the real interaction of `--validate=false` with this? ### What did you expect to happen? I expected `kubectl apply --dry-run=client --validate=false` to be a form of linting without authenticated access ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.33.5-dispatcher Kustomize Version: v5.6.0 ```
label: actionable

title: kubelet does not start when kubelet folder is on ZFS filesystem because of missing cadvisor plugin in 1.36.0
body:
### What happened?

After upgrading to Kubernetes 1.36.0, the kubelet crashes directly after startup on systems that have the `/var/lib/kubelet` folder configured on a ZFS filesystem. The direct error shown in the logs is:

```
E0423 21:45:14.682963  326484 kubelet.go:1821] "Failed to start ContainerManager" err="failed to get rootfs info: failed to get device for dir \"/var/lib/kubelet\": with major: 0, minor: 60: could not find device in cached partitions map"
```

This error is caused by the kubelet not being able to determine the available space for empheral storage, which it normally gets using cadvisor.

After increasing the log level, it seems that this is caused by cadvisor not having access to its ZFS plugin:
```
Apr 23 21:45:14 strike01 kubelet[326484]: I0423 21:45:14.680361  326484 fs.go:406] no plugin found for filesystem type: zfs
```

### What did you expect to happen?

Like Kubernetes 1.35.3 (or 1.35.4 for that matter): I expect the kubelet to startup and work.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

As described above: Ensure `/var/lib/kubelet` is on a ZFS filesystem and start the kubelet with any configuration.

### Anything else we need to know?

I am aware that Kubernetes does not maintain cadvisor and that cadvisor bugs should not be posted here. However, I believe that cadvisor is working correctly, it is just missing its ZFS plugin.

FS plug-ins in cadvisor are introduced in version v0.55.0, before the introduction everything was built-in. Kubernetes 1.36.0 brings cadvisor from version [v0.53.0 → v0.56.0](https://github.com/google/cadvisor/compare/v0.53.0...v0.56.0). It was specifically introduced in https://github.com/google/cadvisor/commit/28ecaa9d9b4aa2ea878f7692a315797c2a9d7a7c

In the PR merging 0.55.1, #135829, I see that some file system extensions are specifically being imported (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/135829/changes#diff-ca41d4fa89358cfbf866e71de1c54ab978a448e805495bf8bca923d85dae31fb), but the ZFS plug-in is missing.

title: HTTP probe documentation doesn't explain edge cases
body:
### What happened?

Kubelet's HTTP readiness/liveness probe follows 301 redirects that change the scheme from HTTP to HTTPS, even when the pod spec explicitly sets `scheme: HTTP`. This causes probes to fail with TLS errors against HTTP-only servers.

The `RedirectChecker` in `pkg/probe/http/http.go` only validates that the redirect hostname matches the original request, but does not validate that the scheme remains unchanged:

```go
// pkg/probe/http/http.go - current code
func RedirectChecker(followNonLocalRedirects bool) func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
    if followNonLocalRedirects {
        return nil
    }
    return func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
        if req.URL.Hostname() != via[0].URL.Hostname() {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        }
        if len(via) >= 10 {
            return errors.New("stopped after 10 redirects")
        }
        return nil  // BUG: Allows scheme changes (HTTP→HTTPS)
    }
}
```

When a server redirects `http://10.42.0.6:8000/health` → `https://10.42.0.6:8000/health` (same hostname, different scheme), the redirect is allowed. The Go HTTP client then attempts a TLS handshake against the HTTP-only server, which fails.

**Kubelet events show the scheme switch:**
```
Warning  Unhealthy  46s  kubelet  Readiness probe failed: Get "http://10.42.0.33:8000/health": connection refused
Warning  Unhealthy  6s   kubelet  Readiness probe failed: Get "https://10.42.0.33:8000/health": EOF
```

**Container logs confirm TLS handshake attempts:**
```
HTTP -> 301 https://10.42.0.33:8000/health
HTTPS DETECTED! TLS ClientHello: 16030105ba01000566
HTTP -> 301 https://10.42.0.33:8000/health
HTTPS DETECTED! TLS ClientHello: 16030105ba01000566
```

Each probe correctly starts with HTTP (from pod spec), but follows the redirect to HTTPS, fails, and repeats indefinitely. The pod never becomes Ready.


### What did you expect to happen?

When a user specifies `scheme: HTTP` in the probe configuration, kubelet should **not** follow redirects that change the scheme to HTTPS. The redirect should be blocked (returning `http.ErrUseLastResponse`), and the probe should succeed with the 301 status code (which is in the 200-399 success range per documentation).

This matches the existing behavior for cross-host redirects, which are correctly blocked.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

**1. Create `redirect_server.py`** - simulates Django's `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT`:
```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
from http.server import HTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler
import sys, time

class RedirectHandler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        host = self.headers.get("Host", "localhost:8000")
        https_url = f"https://{host}{self.path}"
        self.send_response(301)
        self.send_header("Location", https_url)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
        self.end_headers()
        print(f"HTTP -> 301 {https_url}", file=sys.stderr)

    def log_message(self, *args): pass

    def handle(self):
        try:
            self.raw_requestline = self.rfile.readline(65537)
            if self.raw_requestline and self.raw_requestline[0] == 0x16:
                print(f"HTTPS DETECTED! TLS: {self.raw_requestline[:10].hex()}", file=sys.stderr)
                return
            if not self.raw_requestline or not self.parse_request():
                return
            getattr(self, "do_" + self.command, lambda: None)()
            self.wfile.flush()
        except: pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Startup delay 15s...", file=sys.stderr)
    time.sleep(15)
    HTTPServer(("0.0.0.0", 8000), RedirectHandler).serve_forever()
```

**2. Create `Dockerfile`:**
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim
COPY redirect_server.py /app/
CMD ["python3", "-u", "/app/redirect_server.py"]
```

**3. Create `deployment.yaml`:**
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: probe-redirect-bug
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: probe-redirect-bug}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: {app: probe-redirect-bug}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: server
        image: probe-redirect-bug:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Never
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8000
            scheme: HTTP  # Ignored when server redirects to HTTPS
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
          failureThreshold: 30
```

**4. Deploy and observe:**
```bash
docker build -t probe-redirect-bug:latest .
# For k3s:
docker save probe-redirect-bug:latest | sudo k3s ctr images import -
# For other clusters, push to a registry

kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get events -w --field-selector reason=Unhealthy
```

[redirect_server.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25024894/redirect_server.py)
[deployment.yaml](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25024895/deployment.yaml)
[README.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25024897/README.md)

### Anything else we need to know?

### Real-World Impact

This affects Django applications with `SECURE_SSL_REDIRECT = True`, a common production security setting. Django redirects `http://HOST/...` → `https://HOST/...` using the request's Host header, which means the redirect hostname matches the original request.

### Proposed Fix

Add a scheme check to `RedirectChecker`:

```go
func RedirectChecker(followNonLocalRedirects bool) func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
    if followNonLocalRedirects {
        return nil
    }
    return func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
        orig := via[0].URL
        // Block cross-host OR cross-scheme redirects
        if req.URL.Hostname() != orig.Hostname() || req.URL.Scheme != orig.Scheme {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        }
        if len(via) >= 10 {
            return errors.New("stopped after 10 redirects")
        }
        return nil
    }
}
```

$ kubectl version

Kustomize Version: v5.7.1
Server Version: v1.34.3+k3s1
```

</details>

title: Standard connection draining semantics for long-lived HTTP connections
body:
### What would you like to be added?

I would like Gateway API to define standard connection draining semantics for long-lived HTTP connections, especially WebSocket, SSE, and long-lived gRPC/HTTP streams.

Gateway API already supports identifying WebSocket backends through `Service.spec.ports[].appProtocol` values such as `kubernetes.io/ws` and `kubernetes.io/wss`, and Kubernetes EndpointSlice already exposes `serving`, `terminating`, and `ready` endpoint conditions. However, there does not appear to be a portable Gateway API-level policy that describes how implementations should drain long-lived connections during backend Pod termination, Gateway data plane termination, rolling updates, scale-down, or node drain.

This issue is intended to explore whether Gateway API should standardize a small set of connection draining semantics, for example:

- Stop routing new long-lived HTTP connections to backends whose EndpointSlice condition is `terminating: true`.
- Continue serving existing long-lived connections to a terminating backend while `serving: true`, until a configurable drain timeout expires.
- Provide an implementation-independent way to configure a drain timeout for Gateway-managed data planes and/or backend connections.
- Define expected behavior for WebSocket, SSE, and streaming HTTP/gRPC connections during rolling updates and scale-down.
- Clarify whether this belongs in existing route timeout policy, BackendTLSPolicy-style policy attachment, a new policy type, implementation guidance, or conformance documentation.

A possible API direction could be something like a policy that attaches to `Gateway`, `HTTPRoute`, or `Service` backends:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1alphaX
kind: ConnectionDrainPolicy
metadata:
  name: long-lived-http-drain
spec:
  targetRefs:
  - group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
    kind: HTTPRoute
    name: realtime-route
  drainTimeout: 10m
  applyTo:
  - WebSocket
  - ServerSentEvents
  - StreamingHTTP
```

### Why is this needed?

Long-lived HTTP connections behave differently from ordinary request/response HTTP traffic. A WebSocket or streaming request can remain open for minutes or hours. During rolling updates or scale-down, users often want the following behavior:
Existing WebSocket/streaming clients should remain connected to the old backend while it drains.
New connections should be routed to non-terminating backends.
The old backend should be allowed to exit after all connections finish or after a configured drain timeout.
The behavior should be portable across Gateway API implementations.
Today, this behavior is implementation-specific. Some implementations, such as Envoy Gateway, provide graceful shutdown and configurable drain timeouts for their own data plane. Other ingress controllers or service mesh implementations have their own approaches. Kubernetes itself exposes useful primitives through EndpointSlice serving and terminating conditions, but Gateway API does not seem to define how Gateway implementations should use those signals for long-lived HTTP connections.
This creates a portability gap for realtime applications such as:
- collaborative editors
- chat and presence systems
- multiplayer or realtime session services
- AI streaming APIs
- ive transcription
- notification gateways
- dashboards using WebSocket or SSE
- long-lived gRPC streams

Without common semantics, users must rely on controller-specific annotations, custom preStop hooks, sidecars, sticky sessions, or application-level reconnect logic. Those are useful, but they make behavior hard to reason about and hard to migrate across Gateway API implementations.
This proposal is intentionally scoped to graceful draining. It is not proposing transparent migration of an existing TCP/WebSocket connection from one Pod to another after the Pod has already died. That is likely outside the scope of Gateway API and Kubernetes Services. The goal is to standardize drain behavior while the old endpoint or Gateway data plane is still alive.
Related existing primitives and context:
- Kubernetes EndpointSlice serving / terminating / ready conditions
- Kubernetes KEP-1669 Proxy Terminating Endpoints
- Gateway API support for kubernetes.io/ws and kubernetes.io/wss via appProtocol
Existing implementation-specific graceful shutdown / drain behavior in Gateway controllers
I would be happy to help refine the problem statement, write documentation, prototype conformance expectations, or draft a GEP if maintainers think this belongs in Gateway API.

title: kubelet: QoS-level memory.min / memory.low is not cleared after MemoryQoS feature gate is disabled (regression from #138430)
body:
### What happened?

After #138430 re-gated the call to `setMemoryQoS` behind `utilfeature.DefaultFeatureGate.Enabled(kubefeatures.MemoryQoS)`, disabling the `MemoryQoS` alpha feature gate no longer clears stale `memory.min` / `memory.low` values from QoS-level cgroups (`kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice`, `kubepods.slice/kubepods-guaranteed.slice`, etc.) on cgroup v2 unified systems.

Before #138430, `setMemoryQoS` was invoked unconditionally from `UpdateCgroups` on cgroup v2 unified mode. Its zero-out branch at [`pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L303-L308`](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L303-L308) resets `memory.min` / `memory.low` to 0 whenever `memoryReservationPolicy != TieredReservation`, which covers the "feature disabled or policy = None" case. With the gate check added at [L358](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/cm/qos_container_manager_linux.go#L358), that zero-out branch is unreachable whenever the gate is off.

This is the QoS-level analogue of the pod-level regression that #137674 / #137726 already address. #137726 added `ReconcilePodMemoryMin` on `podContainerManagerImpl` but does not touch QoS-level cgroups, so the stale values at the QoS level remain indefinitely on any node that previously ran with the alpha gate enabled and was later rolled back.

### What did you expect to happen?

When MemoryQoS is disabled (feature gate off, or `memoryReservationPolicy = None`), QoS-level `memory.min` / `memory.low` should be reset to 0 on the next `UpdateCgroups` cycle. This matches the explicit assumption in #137674 that "QoS-level cgroups are correctly reset via the periodic `setMemoryQoS()` loop."

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Cgroup v2 unified node.
2. Start kubelet with `--feature-gates=MemoryQoS=true` and `memoryReservationPolicy: HardReservation`.
3. Create a few Burstable pods so that QoS-level values are populated. Verify:
   `cat /sys/fs/cgroup/kubepods.slice/kubepods-burstable.slice/memory.low` → non-zero.
4. Disable the gate by restarting kubelet with `--feature-gates=MemoryQoS=false` (or set `memoryReservationPolicy: None`).
5. After the next `UpdateCgroups` cycle, observe that `memory.low` still carries the previous non-zero value. Restart kubelet and repeat — the value persists.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Closely related: #137674 (pod-level tracking issue), #137726 (pod-level fix), #137889 (earlier removal of `reconcilePodMemoryProtection`), #138431 (motivated #138430).
- The pod-level fix in #137726 does not cover QoS-level cgroups; there is no existing analogue on `qosContainerManagerImpl`.

### Proposed fix options

There are two viable approaches; I would appreciate guidance from sig-node on which shape is preferred:

1. **Keep `setMemoryQoS` unconditional** on cgroup v2 unified mode inside `UpdateCgroups`, and move the feature-gate check *inside* `setMemoryQoS` so it still runs the zero-out branch (L303–L308) but skips the populate branch. Minimal diff; preserves the original cleanup contract.
2. **Add a QoS-level reconcile method** analogous to `ReconcilePodMemoryMin` (#137726) that walks QoS cgroups and zeroes `memory.min` / `memory.low` when the gate is off. Larger diff but symmetric with the pod-level structure.

### Kubernetes version

master at `03779bbd0042` and any release branch that carries the #138430 backports.

/sig node
/area kubelet
/kind bug
/kind regression

title: Some crashed or OOMKilled containers fail to restart in v1.35
body:
### What happened?

After upgrading Kubernetes from v1.34.2 to v1.35.0, we observed a scenario where a pod with multiple containers does not restart a crashed application container, leaving the pod in an Error state indefinitely.

This behavior was not observed on v1.34.2. Reverting the kubelet back to v1.34.2 causes the issue to disappear.

**Observed Behavior:**
The main container terminates but never restarts:
```
State:          Terminated
  Reason:       Error
  Exit Code:    2
  Started:      Tue, 27 Jan 2026 16:11:01 +0000
  Finished:     Tue, 10 Feb 2026 11:08:55 +0000
Ready:          False
Restart Count:  0
```

The sidecar container continues to run normally:
```
State:          Running
Started:        Tue, 27 Jan 2026 16:10:54 +0000
Ready:          True
Restart Count:  0
```

Pod conditions show:
```
Conditions:
  Type                        Status
  PodReadyToStartContainers   True
  Initialized                 True
  Ready                       False
  ContainersReady             False
  PodScheduled                True
```

No useful logs or errors appear in `kubectl describe pod` output, events, or `kubelet` logs.

**Notes:**
- This issue seems to only affect pods with more than one container
- We are unsure whether it's just pods with an `initContainer` or does it also apply to `container` sidecars
- Manually killing the process in the sidecar container or deleting the pod helps getting it back to working state
- `RestartAllContainersOnContainerExits` is not enabled

**Possibly related?**
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/134345

### What did you expect to happen?

Containers should reliably restart every time they crash.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The best way we found to reproduce this is by running a pod with 2 containers: an initContainer with `restartPolicy: Always` and an application container that we manually crash with `kill 1` command.
It might not work right first time, but we managed to reproduce this multiple times getting pods stuck in Error state that they never recover from automatically.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: setcap build image shouldn't require a shell
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Building with a more vanilla setcap image shouldn't require a shell in the image to run the command 


in `build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile`

```sh
# We apply cap_net_bind_service so that kube-apiserver can be run as
# non-root and still listen on port less than 1024
RUN setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /${BINARY}
```

this command requires the `SETCAP_IMAGE` have a shell in order to:
1) RUN a command that isn't in the form of ["/usr/sbin/setcap", "..."] 
2) shell expand the `${BINARY}` argument


### Why is this needed?

By making this change you can eliminate the need of having a shell in the setcap image:


```diff
diff --git a/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile b/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
index 27129d29bd9..acfe8c26f22 100644
--- a/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
+++ b/build/server-image/kube-apiserver/Dockerfile
@@ -20,11 +20,11 @@ ARG SETCAP_IMAGE
 # to setup qemu for the builder.
 FROM --platform=linux/$BUILDARCH ${SETCAP_IMAGE}
 ARG BINARY
-COPY --chmod=755 ${BINARY} /${BINARY}
+COPY --chmod=755 ${BINARY} /set_cap_binary
 # We apply cap_net_bind_service so that kube-apiserver can be run as
 # non-root and still listen on port less than 1024
-RUN setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /${BINARY}
+RUN ["setcap", "cap_net_bind_service=+ep", "/set_cap_binary"]
 
 FROM --platform=linux/$TARGETARCH ${BASEIMAGE}
 ARG BINARY
-COPY --from=0 /${BINARY} /usr/local/bin/${BINARY}
+COPY --from=0 /set_cap_binary /usr/local/bin/${BINARY}
```

title: Kubelet regression in 1.32, 1.31 and possibly 1.33 and 1.34 where pods get stuck in RunContainerError on OS with cgroupv1
body:
### What happened?

We observed a Kubelet regression in 1.32 and 1.31 (and similar symptoms in 1.33 and 1.34) where pods get stuck in `RunContainerError` on Rocky Linux 8.6 OS which uses cgroup v1. While upgrading Kubernetes from 1.30 to 1.31 and 1.32, we observe the issue once we put the node out of maintenance mode.

The issue is observed with Containerd 1.7 and 1.6 as well.

We initially opened this issue https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/138388 however at the time we didn't know what caused the regression and what versions were affected. We performed a git bisect (using GKE internal builds) and identified the regression was introduced in PR [#131018](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131018). This commit was merged into 1.34 and backported all the way to 1.31. Kubelet works perfectly in the commits immediately preceding this PR.

Following this commit, we observe a massive spike in masked paths. Given our 96-core machines, the `thermal_throttle` paths alone add 96 new entries to the maskedPaths array for every container:

```
crictl inspect 4a44698096076 | jq '.info.config.linux.security_context.masked_paths'
[
  "/proc/asound",
  "/proc/acpi",
  "/proc/interrupts",
  "/proc/kcore",
  "/proc/keys",
  "/proc/latency_stats",
  "/proc/timer_list",
  "/proc/timer_stats",
  "/proc/sched_debug",
  "/proc/scsi",
  "/sys/firmware",
  "/sys/devices/virtual/powercap",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/thermal_throttle",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu1/thermal_throttle",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu2/thermal_throttle",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu3/thermal_throttle",
[...]
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu94/thermal_throttle",
  "/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu95/thermal_throttle"
]
```

We suspect that this high volume of masked paths is causing kernel-level starvation or resource exhaustion on our cgroup v1 / Rocky 8.6 nodes when scheduling a large number of multi-container pods.

So far we compiled,  we compiled a custom Kubelet that breaks the loop after adding the first `thermal_throttle` path. Under load testing, the system remained completely stable with this patch:

```
v1.32.13-gke.100) ~/gke-internal/kubernetes $ git diff
diff --git a/pkg/securitycontext/util.go b/pkg/securitycontext/util.go
index 5e000f93333..f1889a8cff8 100644
--- a/pkg/securitycontext/util.go
+++ b/pkg/securitycontext/util.go
@@ -213,6 +213,7 @@ var (
                        path := fmt.Sprintf("/sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu%d/thermal_throttle", cpu)
                        if _, err := os.Stat(path); err == nil {
                                maskedPaths = append(maskedPaths, path)
+                               break
                        }
                }
 
(v1.32.13-gke.100) ~/gke-internal/kubernetes $ 
``` 

The following kernel settings currently resolve the issue so it is not tracking kernel memory:
  * Set the `cgroup.memory=nokmem` config during the OS upgrade.
  * Reboot the node as part of the OS upgrade process.
  * Upgrade K8s to 1.31

Not tracking kernel memory to mitigate this issue is a big NO for us.

Questions & Asks for the Community: 

The PR https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/131018 that introduced this regression states that it "Mitigates potential Thermal Side-Channel Vulnerability Exploit," linking to a Moby security advisory ([GHSA-6fw5-f8r9-fgfm](https://github.com/moby/moby/security/advisories/GHSA-6fw5-f8r9-fgfm)). However, this link currently returns a 404 error, making it difficult for us to evaluate the exact threat model.

- Could you provide more context on the specific vulnerability (#131018 mitigates) since the advisory link is dead?

- What are the practical security consequences of bypassing or reverting this specific thermal_throttle masking change?

- Is there an appetite to introduce a feature gate or Kubelet flag to bypass this specific path masking for environments where it causes kernel starvation?

Any suggestions, alternative fixes, or guidance from the OSS community would be greatly appreciated.

### What did you expect to happen?

in 1.31, 1.32, 1.33 and 1.34, cgroupv1 is not yet deprecated https://kubernetes.io/blog/2024/08/13/kubernetes-v1-31-release/#cgroup-v1-enters-the-maintenance-mode  (although it was put in maintenance mode), Kubelet should not yet be unhappy with cgroupv1 until it is fully deprecated. The expectation is that this regression should not happen in Kubelet 1.32, 1.31, 1.33 and 1.34.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Rocky Linux 8.6 OS with cgroup v1

K8s version 1.32.13

Run the following deployment 

```
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:

title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Readiness Observations & Recommendations (Research)
body:
This issue shares research-based observations on post-quantum cryptography (PQC) readiness
in Kubernetes, based solely on publicly available code and documentation.

This is NOT a vulnerability report and does not include exploitation, attack paths, or
sensitive configuration details. The intent is awareness, future-readiness, and community
discussion aligned with NIST PQC transition guidance.

Observations:
• Cryptographic usage is distributed across multiple layers
• There is no centralized crypto inventory or ownership map
• No defined crypto agility or PQC migration framework
• No governance-level visibility into algorithm lifecycle

Recommendations:
• Consider adding a crypto inventory layer
• Define crypto ownership and lifecycle policy
• Track NIST PQC migration readiness
• Introduce crypto agility abstractions
• Document PQC roadmap for operators

Why this matters:
Quantum-safe transitions are multi-year efforts. Early visibility reduces long-term risk.

Happy to refine or contribute to documentation if helpful.

title: StatefulSet pod revisions not updated when MaxUnavailableStatefulSet enabled
body:
### What happened?

I decided to open this issue after investigating https://github.com/stackabletech/trino-operator/issues/854.

The high level description of the problem is that the stateful set controller doesn't update the pods according to the latest STS revision and the pods are left crashlooping **if the first revision is faulty** and can never become available. This doesn't happen if the `MaxUnavailableStatefulSet` feature is disabled.

Unfortunately I cannot create a much simpler example, but I attach the relevant controller log messages below.

Based on these logs you can see that:

1. The Stackable Operator for Trino (`trino-op` from now on) creates two `StatefulSet` objects with a single replica. They both expose the same problem, so for simplicity, I will use only one of them from now on (`trino-coordinator-default`).
2. The initial revision of this sts is `trino-coordinator-default-5f5598d4c8`. This first STS  revision has a faulty command args  and can never become available.
3. The `trino-op` updates the sts rapidly to the revision `trino-coordinator-default-787556ff59`. Now the STS command args are correct and the pods should be able to become ready.
4. The pod created initially is never updated so it never becomes ready.

To summarize my understanding, the sts revision is never updated if the pod never becomes ready, and the pod doesn't become ready because it has an old revision.

In the logs you see that `currentRevision` is never the same as `updateRevision`:

```
I0304 15: 25:06.514308       1 stateful_set_control.go: 146]"StatefulSet revisions" statefulSet = "kuttl-test-distinct-turtle/trino-coordinator-default" currentRevision = "trino-coordinator-default-5f5598d4c8" updateRevision = "trino-coordinator-default-787556ff59"
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod should become ready according to the `updateRevision` of the sts.
Again, this was indeed the case until `MaxUnavailableStatefulSet` feature gate was enabled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

I can reproduce this bug using the `trino-op` but unfortunately I don't have a minimal example.

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/html.py


### Documentation problem

Several functions in `pandas/io/html.py` have docstrings that violate [PEP 257](https://peps.python.org/pep-0257/) and pandas documentation guidelines. Flagged violations include:

- `D400`: Docstring summary should end with a period  
- `D205`: Docstring summary should be followed by a blank line  
- `D401`: First line of docstring should be in imperative mood  

These inconsistencies reduce clarity and hinder automated validation.



### Suggested fix for documentation

Standardize docstring formatting based on `flake8-docstrings` and `pydocstyle` feedback to meet pandas’ documentation standards. This includes:

- Adding missing punctuation and spacing  
- Rewriting summaries for clarity and imperative voice  
- Ensuring consistent style across the module  

This fix is scoped to documentation and does not impact functionality.

title: BUG: `record_prefix` ignored when `record_path` is empty
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

_s = pd.Series([    {"k": f"{i}", "m": "q"} for i in range(5)
])

pd.json_normalize(_s,record_prefix="T")
```

### Issue Description

The `record_prefix` is completely ignored and the resulting columns are note renamed.

```
   k  m
0  0  q
1  1  q
2  2  q
3  3  q
4  4  q
```

The issue is in [L517-L527](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/io/json/_normalize.py#L517-L527) where a short cut is taken for speed.
One option to fix this would be to pass the `record_prefix` as `prefix` to `nested_to_record`.

This is hidden in the documentation example by using a positional argument for the record path

```
    >>> data = {"A": [1, 2]}
    >>> pd.json_normalize(data, "A", record_prefix="Prefix.")
        Prefix.0
    0          1
    1          2
```


### Expected Behavior

The prefix should be applied (or an explicit warning be given)

```
  T.k T.m
0   0   q
1   1   q
2   2   q
3   3   q
4   4   q
```

body:

import pandas as pd

s2 = pd.Series([1,2], name=pd.to_datetime('2027'))

print(s1.combine_first(s3))
```

### Issue Description

`s1.combine_first(s3)` fails because `s3.name` is a datetime anterior to `s1.name`.

It does not throw any error in pandas version < 3.

title: fillna for np.float64(np.nan)
body:
I like `pd.Float64Dtype()` and other pandas datatypes, but one small glitch found in below minimal case:

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame([(2, 1), (0, 0), (0, None)], columns=('a', 'b'))
df = df.astype(pd.Float64Dtype())

print(df['b'] / df['a'])
# 0     0.5
# 1     NaN
# 2    <NA>
# dtype: Float64

print((df['b'] / df['a']).fillna(0))
# 0    0.5
# 1    NaN

title: DOC: rendering bug - `{{ }}` shown instead of `{ }` across API documentation
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_sas.html
https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_table.html
... **seemingly all pages**

### Documentation problem

The issue appears in multiple places across the documentation (e.g., parameter descriptions and examples where `{{ }}` is rendered instead of `{ }`). We should identify and fix the root cause or update all affected occurrences; otherwise, the docs will remain inconsistent and continue to show invalid Python syntax in other sections.

Related to https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/64394.

Just in `reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html` ([link](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.read_csv.html)), there are at least:
- Double braces `{{ }}` appear in code examples instead of normal Python dict braces `{ }`, producing invalid syntax (e.g., `dtype={{"Value": float}}`).

- The `date_format` example also uses double braces:  
  `date_format={{"col 2": "%d/%m/%Y", "col 3": "%a %d %b %Y"}}`.

- Parameter type description for `dtype` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{Hashable dtype}}`.

- Parameter type description for `converters` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableCallable}}`.

- Parameter type description for `na_values` renders incorrectly as:  
  `dict of {{HashableIterable}}`.

- Enum values for `engine` render incorrectly as:  
  `engine {{‘c’, ‘python’, ‘pyarrow’}}`.

- Enum values for `quoting` render incorrectly as:  
  `{{0 or csv.QUOTE_MINIMAL, 1 or csv.QUOTE_ALL, ...}}`.

- Header renaming description renders placeholders incorrectly as:  
  `".{{count}}"`.

- Placeholder examples for unnamed columns render incorrectly as:  
  `"Unnamed: {{i}}"` and `"Unnamed: {{i}}_level_{{level}}"`.

- Several dictionary examples throughout the page use `{{ }}` instead of `{ }`, which makes the shown Python code invalid.

### Suggested fix for documentation

I assume the double braces were originally used to escape literal `{}` in docstrings that passed through a .format()/Substitution step. Since the formatting step is seemingly no longer applied (TBC?) in the current doc build, the escapes now leak into the rendered docs, so they should be replaced across the repo with normal braces only if we can confirm they're no longer necessary or we need to fix the build step.

title: ENH: Add DataFrame.memory_report() for actionable dtype optimization suggestions
body: ### Feature Type - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas ### Problem Description DataFrame.memory_usage() tells you how much memory a DataFrame uses, but gives no guidance on why or what to do about it. Users who want to optimize memory must: - Manually inspect each column's dtype - Know the integer/float downcast rules by heart - Manually check cardinality for object columns - Write their own loops to apply changes This is a very common pain point — especially for data engineers and analysts working with medium-to-large datasets who hit memory pressure and have no built-in tool to diagnose it. ### Feature Description A new method DataFrame.memory_report() that: 1. Analyzes every column's current dtype and actual value range 2. Suggests the smallest safe dtype for each column 3. Explains why each suggestion is safe (value range, cardinality ratio) 4. Returns a rich MemoryReport object that is both human-readable and 5. machine-readable 6. Never modifies the DataFrame — purely diagnostic, zero side effects def memory_report( self, verbose: bool = True, category_threshold: float = 0.5, check_datetimes: bool = True, ) -> MemoryReport: """ Analyze memory usage and suggest safe dtype optimizations. Parameters ---------- verbose : bool, default True If True, print the full report to stdout. category_threshold : float, default 0.5 Suggest ``category`` dtype when unique ratio is below this value. For example, 0.5 means fewer than 50% unique values → suggest category. check_datetimes : bool, default True Attempt to detect datetime-parseable strings in object columns. Samples up to 200 rows to avoid scanning very large columns. Returns ------- MemoryReport Structured report with per-column diagnostics. Supports: - ``report.to_dataframe()`` — machine-readable table - ``report.apply(df)`` — apply all suggestions, returns new df - ``report.actionable`` — list of columns with suggestions - ``report.high_impact`` — columns with >= 50% savings potential """ ### Alternative Solutions df.info(memory_usage='deep'). This is the closest native.But no guidance on how to fix it. ### Additional Context Design Decisions Zero side effects. memory_report() never modifies the DataFrame. Applying suggestions is always an explicit opt-in via report.apply(df). Safe-only suggestions. Every suggestion is lossless by default: Integer downcasts are validated against actual min/max values Float32 suggestions are validated: values are cast to float32 and checked for overflow before recommending apply() wraps each conversion in a try/except and warns on failure — it never raises Null awareness. The report flags columns with nulls so users know before applying dtype changes that may affect null representation. Overflow guard for floats. The implementation detects when a finite float64 value would become ±inf after float32 cast, and keeps float64. Composable return type. Returning a MemoryReport rather than just printing means the output is usable in notebooks, CI pipelines, and data quality checks.

title: ENH: High-performance implementation function for appending rows to a dataframe
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I receive real-time financial data using a dataframe. While pandas 1.x allows appending rows via df.loc[new_index]=..., pandas 2 does not support this operation. Therefore, I  implemented a function to  enables row appending, and this function is highly efficient.



### Feature Description

append row to dataframe 

### Alternative Solutions


```python
def df_append_row(df: 'pd.DataFrame', row_index: 'pd.Timestamp|pd.NaT|int|None' = None, extend_size=1_000, *, ffill: bool = False) -> None:
    mgr = df._mgr
    df_len = len(df)
    
    for blk in mgr.blocks:
        # blk.values is data array
        arr: 'np.ndarray' = blk.values
        arr_shape = arr.shape
        cached_array: 'np.ndarray|None' = getattr(blk, "mx_cache_d", None)
        if cached_array is None or cached_array.shape[-1] <= arr_shape[-1]:
            new_shape = list(arr_shape)
            new_shape[-1] += extend_size
            cached_array = np.empty(new_shape, arr.dtype)
            cached_array[..., :arr_shape[-1]] = arr
            if arr.dtype.kind == 'f':  # if dtype is np.floatN: set to np.nan
                cached_array[..., arr_shape[-1]:] = np.nan
            setattr(blk, "mx_cache_d", cached_array)
        blk.values = cached_array[..., :arr_shape[-1] + 1]
        if ffill:
            blk.values[-1] = blk.values[-2]

    index = mgr.axes[1]
    if isinstance(index, pd.DatetimeIndex):
        cached_index: 'pd.DatetimeIndex' = getattr(mgr, "mx_cache_i", None)
        if cached_index is None or len(cached_index) <= df_len:
            cached_array = np.zeros(df_len + extend_size, dtype='datetime64[ns]')  
            cached_array[:df_len] = index._data._ndarray
            cached_index = pd.DatetimeIndex(data=cached_array, copy=False, name=index.name)  
            setattr(mgr, "mx_cache_i", cached_index)  
        # index._data._ndarray=cached_index[:len(index)+1] # _ndarray not changed
        # setattr(index._data,"_ndarray",cached_index[:len(index)+1])

        new_index = cached_index[:df_len + 1]  # new_index = pd.DatetimeIndex(cached_index[:df_len + 1], copy=False, name=index.name)
        if row_index is None:
            row_index = _NaT_i64  
        elif isinstance(row_index, pd.Timestamp):
            row_index = row_index.to_datetime64().view(np.int64)
        new_index._data._ndarray[-1] = row_index
        mgr.axes[1] = new_index
    elif isinstance(index, pd.RangeIndex):  #
        r: 'range' = index._range
        index._range = range(r.start, r.stop + r.step, r.step)
        _ = getattr(index, "_cache", {}).pop("_data", None) 
    else:
        raise NotImplemented(f"df_append_row:The type of index ({type(index)}) is not supported. [DatetimeIndex/RangeIndex]")

    df._reset_cache()
    df._clear_item_cache()
```

### Problem Description

I wish I could use Pandas to directly read .conll files, a common format in NLP for tasks like named entity recognition and POS tagging, without writing custom parsers.

### Feature Description

Add a `pandas.read_conll` function to parse `.conll` files into a DataFrame. It should handle tab-separated data, blank lines for sentence boundaries, and optional comments (e.g., lines starting with #).

Proposed API. 
```
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_conll('data.conll', columns=['token', 'pos', 'chunk', 'ner'], group_by_sentence=False)
```

Key Features
- Parse tab-separated .conll files into a DataFrame.
- Support custom column names.
- Optionally group by sentence with a sentence_id column.
- Skip comments and handle blank lines.
- Support common formats (e.g., CoNLL-2003, CoNLL-U).



### Alternative Solutions

- Use pandas.read_csv with sep='\t' and manually process blank lines/comments, but this is prone to errors.
- Use the conllu package to parse CoNLL-U files, but it requires additional dependencies and conversion to DataFrames.
- Write custom parsers, which is time consuming and not reusable.

)

title: angular strange behavior when migrating from angular 20.0.x to 20.1.x regarding @angular/compiler and/or @angular/compiler-cli
body:
### Which @angular/* package(s) are the source of the bug?

compiler-cli, compiler

### Is this a regression?

Yes

### Description

At our company we use @angular with custom cdn.
This means we make @angular js bundles with webpack and use externals.
The angular cli project is hooked to @angular-builders/custom-webpack
We also have @my-company custom angular libraries (ng-packagr) which also render a js bundel in a custom cdn. These use compilation mode partial. 
This work perfectly up until @angular 20.0.x.
So the problems i encountered:
- some elements not renderer well and causing other elements not to be renders
- issue with viewchild
- issues with mat buttons in mat dialogs

I could isolate the problem to @angular/compiler and/or @angular/compiler-cli (both versions need to be the same). I did this by gradually updating each package to 21.1.

If we use compilation mode full in the \@my-company libraries then it works. But I can't just move to this system as we also have third party libraries which are partially compiled.

When I read the documentation there seems to be something new in the compiler regarding 'optimized template compilation'. So my guess the problem is related to this area.

Probably some elements are jitted but something doesnt work out and is being skipped?

It's a critical problem because we have 50+ applications running with this architecture (externals and cdn-like bundles. We wouldn't like to lock on 20.0.x.

title: [data] Always align to 64 bytes when serialize buffer to ensuring downstream consumers get properly aligned memory pointers
body:
when i use raydata to process the case: read from lance tableA and write it to a new table lanceB (table have a decimal128 type field), i encounter a error: "Memory pointer from external source (e.g, FFI) is not aligned with the specified scalar type. Before importing buffer through FFI, please make sure the allocation is aligned";

After seeing the code, i found the reason is: if the column have less data(less than 2048) ray will serialize this buffer with 8-byte alignment (When writing to a LANCE table, LANCE requires that the decimal128 type must be 16-byte aligned)，so it will fail;

There is two way to fix this problem:
	1. before writing lance, check whether the buffer is 16-byte or 64-byte alignment, if not, reconstruct pyarrow.buffer, then write it to lance
	2. Always align to 64 bytes when ray serialize buffer, or can we add a dynamic config that control the 64-byte alignment threshold [kMajorBufferSize](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/python/ray/includes/serialization.pxi#L13) [PS: this method may causing spase waste, but if there are few buffers smaller than 64 bytes, does the wasting is acceptable?]

From my perspective, I lean towards Option 2 (ensuring 64-byte alignment during buffer serialization) for two reasons:
   1. If downstream consumers have to reconstruct the buffer（option 1 ）, it also leads to memory waste and requires redundant implementation across different consumers.
   2. Ensuring 64-byte alignment upfront guarantees optimal SIMD performance for downstream usage (though the performance gains may be modest given the small data volume)

```ruby
class RankingEnv(gym.Env):
    def __init__(self, config: dict):
      super().__init__()
      self.coins = config['df']['tic'].unique()
      features_col = config['df'].columns.difference(['date','tic','score','close_growth(%)'])

      self.df=config['df'].groupby('date')
      self.dates = list(self.df.groups.keys())

      self.observation_space = gym.spaces.Dict({coin: gym.spaces.Box(low=-np.inf, high=np.inf, shape=(len(features_col),), dtype=np.float64) for coin in self.coins})
      self.action_space = gym.spaces.Dict({coin: gym.spaces.Box(low=np.float64(1.0), high=np.float64(len(self.coins)), shape=(1,), dtype=np.float64) for coin in self.coins})#actions are the scores

    def step(self, action):
      group = self.df.get_group(self.dates[self.time])
      true_scores = group.set_index('tic')['score'].to_dict()
      # The indexes are according to predicted score and the values are true score!(Sorting true score by predicted score)
      scores = [true_scores[coin] for coin in sorted(action, key=action.get, reverse=True)]
      ideal_scores = sorted(true_scores.values(), reverse=True) #This is just the True_score as list

      dcg = self.calculate_dcg(scores)
      idcg = self.calculate_dcg(ideal_scores)
      reward = dcg/idcg # reward = ndcg

      self.time+=1
      terminated = self.time >= len(self.dates)
      info = {}
      return self._get_obs() if not terminated else None, reward, terminated, False, info

    def calculate_dcg(self, scores):
      dcg = 0.0
      for i in range(len(scores)):
        dcg += (2 ** scores[i] - 1) / np.log2(i + 2)
      return dcg

    def reset(self, *, seed: Optional[int] = None, options: Optional[dict] = None):
      super().reset(seed=seed,options=options)
      self.time = 0
      info={}
      return self._get_obs() ,info

    def _get_obs(self):
      group = self.df.get_group(self.dates[self.time])
      obs = group.drop(['date','score','close_growth(%)'], axis=1)

      obs = obs.set_index('tic').agg(lambda x: np.array(x.tolist()), axis=1).to_dict()
      
      return obs

    def render(self):
        pass

    def close(self):
        pass

title: [Bug] Possible tune / core bug related to correct resuming of trials on a dynamic cluster
body:
### Search before asking

- [X] I searched the [issues](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues) and found no similar issues.


### Ray Component

Ray Core, Ray Tune

### What happened + What you expected to happen

I ve had a discussion on slack with @krfricke  about a recent tune bugfix that came with this PR (https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/20536) which is among other things concerned with  correct resuming of trials... I myself always had problems in my setup with resume after a few days, so I installed the latest master nightly build  which included that PR and started running some tune session on my cluster. It went smoothly and I thought that bug has solved my problem, but then I got the following "Reset" on the night from 22nd to 23rd. 

Attached you find two pictures from the validation loss for a tune job with 70 tune trials (I run 7 discrete settings with tune.GridSearch() and num_samples=10, so 10 repeats per grid point and 70 total).
 ![training_run_step](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6616661/150848720-16831136-a35b-4ca5-9013-10c7abfc8049.png)
![training_run](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6616661/150848737-663c9d83-fa83-4a42-94db-ef81b86efd5f.png)

You can see that a bunch of trials get reset to the beginning and start over. In the second plot vs walltime it shows that trials stopped working on Jan 22nd .. they then stalled for a while and are only now being reset . 

I should say something about my somewhat peculiar cluster setup: I run on a SGE grid engine where I have 24 hour worker slots .. what I do currently is I have one ray master node that is permanently on a separate machine. On this machine I start ray via 
`subprocess.run(["ray",  "start" ,"--head" ,"--num-cpus=1" , "--num-gpus=0", "--temp-dir=%s" % ray_logdir], stdout=subprocess.PIPE)`
which works as the master node.

Additionally I run a cronjob which creates 3 new worker nodes as SGE slots every hour, and 3 workers crash every hour when their respective SGE slot ends.. so every hour 3 workers are basically crashing, and 3 new workers are added to ray.

On the worker nodes, I execute
`os.system("ray start --address='%s' --redis-password='5241590000000000' --num-cpus=1 --num-gpus=0 --temp-dir=%s" % (head_ip, ray_logdir))`
to connect to the master node.

Furthermore, on the master node, I then call a python script which first executes `ray.init()` to connect to the cluster and then `tune.rune( )` to run the tune trials.

Because I add 3 workers per hour, and each is 24 hour long, I get a total of 72 nodes permanently on, which can handle my 70 trials. So I have continuous crashing+resuming, which means I rely on correct resuming .. as you can see resuming worked perfectly until the hickup on jan 22/23 . Now, the remaining few trials are still at a standstill and so their progress basically stopped at jan 22/23rd wth the exception of the one trial that is running on the head node. The cluster status tells me 70/70 trials are running, which is definately not the case.. the majority is still stopped and the ones that are running have been reset to the beginning.
 Any idea what this could be or how I could debug this? I really want to solve this... in my opinion it should be possible to set up ray to be stable even if the cluster status is as dynamic as in my case.


**UPDATE**: I just killed the tune job on the head node, left ray running, and restarted the tune job with -resume .. it actually failed to restart with : 
`
Failed to get the system config for raylet because it is dead. Worker will terminate. Status: GrpcUnavailable: RPC Error message: failed to connect to all addresess; RPC Error details:`

I also found a few "too many open files" errors in raylet.err, could they have something to do with this? Does this relate to the log files that are created ? My log folder size from this 1 week of running is 30 GB with tons of files and I have used log_to_file=True. I am currently running again with the option "log_to_file=False", and see what happens. 
I have over 1900 log files in the logdir of the ray session, and over 900 files in the "old" subdirectory. The vast majority of the 30 GB comes from  hundreds of raylet files which are each 80 MB.

**UPDATE2**: 
After running a second time for a week, with "log_to_file=False" (but resume=True probably has overwritten this) the same errors appear and the system seems to be hanging again. Another error I just now discovered is in dashboard.log, of the type:


`2022-01-24 17:31:43,188 ERROR node_head.py:241 -- Error updating node stats of 6ae37dcaf2c024fba86ceb92c1d7b9dd6aed518a0b8c1cf17e956ce9.
Traceback (most recent call last):
    raise _create_rpc_error(self._cython_call._initial_metadata,
grpc.aio._call.AioRpcError: <AioRpcError of RPC that terminated with:
        status = StatusCode.UNAVAILABLE
        details = "failed to connect to all addresses"
        debug_error_string = "{"created":"@1643041903.188611088","description":"Failed to pick subchannel","file":"src/core/ext/filters/client_channel/client_channel.cc","file_line":3134,"referenced_errors":[{"created":"@1643041903.188609397","description":"failed to connect to all addresses","file":"src/core/lib/transport/error_utils.cc","file_line":163,"grpc_status":14}]}"`

Any ideas?

### Versions / Dependencies

2.0.0 nightly build (from ~17th of january 2022), python 3.89, scientific linux 7

### Reproduction script

Currently no script available.

### Anything else

This isse has occured multiple times, but I thought the latest bugfixes with the above mentioned pull release would have fixed it

### Are you willing to submit a PR?

- [ ] Yes I am willing to submit a PR!

body:
### What happened?

When I configured a Pod with startupProbe but without a readinessProbe, the pod will take extra time (40-60 seconds) to be ready.
For example, if the startupProbe is configured as below, and readinessProbe is not configured at all

```
startupProbe:
  exec:
    command:
    - echo
    - started
  failureThreshold: 3
  initialDelaySeconds: 20
  periodSeconds: 5
  successThreshold: 1
  timeoutSeconds: 1
```

Then the pod will be ready after around 20 seconds as expected, but will take extra seconds to be ready as shown below:
